titleStmt.title: Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) using Deferred Abort

analytic.title: Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) using Deferred Abort

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper extends the Abort-and-Restart (AR) model by defining the Deferred Abort (DA) model, Both models support Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP). Higher priority tasks sometimes do not need an immediate abort to meet their deadlines. The technique of deferred preemption is employed for the DA model, which provides better schedulability and dominates the non-preemptive model. In this paper, we also provide a final non-preemptive region assignment, and a heuristic priority assignment scheme. In the experimental evaluation, the schedulability of the DA model demonstrated a clear improvement compared to the AR model.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Abort-and-Restart is a scheme [16], [17] to support Priority-based Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP). P-FRP has been introduced as a new functional programming scheme [2] for real-time systems. It combines the property of atomic execution from Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) [14], and supports priority assignment. Atomic execution means that tasks execute independently and no resource is locked by any task. To achieve this property of P-FRP, higher priority tasks can preempt lower priority tasks and the lower priority tasks are aborted and restarted after the higher priority tasks have finished execution. In the classical preemptive model, the lower priority tasks continue their execution but it is different for P-FRP; the lower priority tasks restart as new. Abort-and-Restart is the key operation for P-FRP so we call it the Abort-and-Restart (AR) model in this paper.

In the AR model, tasks cannot access resources directly. Rather, tasks make copies of the resource at the beginning of their execution. The updated data is then copied back into the system once the tasks have completed their execution. In some situations, higher priority tasks preempt lower priority tasks. Once the higher priority tasks have completed execution, the lower priority tasks are aborted and restarted. The operation of abort-and-restart is to delete the old copy of the resource, and take a new copy from the system. The classical preemptive model must deal with the problem of resource sharing. These problems can bring serious consequences. They may lead to inaccurate data, misses deadlines or deadlock. To cater for these problems various forms of priority inheritance and priority ceiling protocols have been developed [12], [13]. One advantage of the AR model is that it does not face these problems because tasks do not access resources directly. The disadvantage is that aborted tasks delete the old copy of the resource and restart as new, hence the time spent before preemption is wasted. In this paper, we call this wasted time, the abort cost.

div.head: A. Motivation
div.p: Nowadays, computers have more power of execution than before. In concurrent programming, sometimes programmers consider how to enhance the correctness of programs rather than reduce their overheads. For a real-time system, it is more complicated because of timing constraints and priorities. A concurrency control mechanism for a system is important because it affects the correctness and the schedulability.

The AR model provides strong correctness guarantees on dealing with shared resources. And it also supports FRP which has been used for the domains of computer animation, computer vision, robotics and control systems [7]. Original FRP cannot be used for real-time systems but P-FRP has rectified this. Hence the AR model is a scheme to support P-FRP.

A real-time database system can be simply defined as a database system with timing constraints [9]. The system receives a high demand of requests and the responses are required to be sent out before their deadlines. A transactional memory can handle shared resource in a convenient way, and the AR scheme can be applied to it. For example, all transactions must be consistent and up-to-date for the stock market. The AR model has the properties of atomic execution and preemption. A transaction will not conflict with another transaction, and an urgent transaction can be execute as soon as possible.

Real-time Java is designed to allow programmers to develop a real-time application using the Java language. Preemptible Atomic Regions (PAR) are a new concurrency control abstraction for real-time systems [8]. The basic notions of the AR model and the PAR model are similar but PAR makes a log of shared resource and then the state of resource will be rolled back if the task is preempted. The paper [8] introduced the example of PAR for real-time Java. In other words, the AR model has been implemented in a common programming language.

div.head: B. Contributions and Organisation
div.p: This paper introduces an alternative scheme to improve the schedulability of the AR model. We call the scheme the deferred abort (DA). We show that the AR model and the non-preemptive model do not dominate each other, but are both dominated by the DA model. We provide a means of calculating the required final non-preemptive region for the DA model. Lastly, an effective priority assignment scheme is provided for the DA model. Experiment shows the DA model has a clear improvement in terms of schedulability.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND RELATED WORK
div.p: The system model is built on the fixed priority scheduling of a set of sporadic tasks on a single processor. Each task consists of a potentially unbounded sequence of jobs.
The notations and formal definitions used in this paper are listed as follows:

div.head: N
div.p: the number of tasks. τ i any given task in the system. C i the worst-case execution time for τ i (also referred to as WCET). D i deadline for τ i . R i response time for τ i . Ci j the new value for the WCET of τ j , the biggest abort cost is picked between τ j and τ i (see equation 1). CDA i,j similar to Ci j but for the DA model (see equation 9). hp (i) set of task of higher priority than τ i . hep (i) higher or equal to the priority of τ i . lp (j) lower than the priority of τ j .
In general we allow constrained deadlines, although previous work and many of the examples in this paper have implicit deadlines. We restrict implementation to single processor systems.

div.head: A. Abort-and-Restart approach
div.p: The Abort-and-Restart (AR) model [10], [11] is a predictable implementation scheme for P-FRP. The classical preemptive model does not fit with P-FRP although it is similar to the AR model except for the operation of abort-and-restart. In the classical model, preempted tasks continue their job once higher priority tasks completed execution. The key concept of the AR model is that lower priority tasks are preempted and aborted by releases of higher priority tasks. Once the higher priority tasks have completed, the lower priority task are restarted as new.

Consider Table I; there is a 2-task task-set. τ 1 is the highest priority task and has 3 ticks for WCET (Worst-case execution time). Task τ 2 has 4 ticks for WCET. In Figure 1, τ 2 is released at 0 and executes until time 3, because of the arrival of τ 1 , τ 2 is aborted at 3. τ 1 finishes its job at time 6 and τ 2 is restarted as a new job so the spent time between 0 and 3 is wasted. In the AR model, the abort cost can modelled [18] by using the following equation:
div.formula: Ci j = C j + max ∀k∈hepi lpj C k (1)
div.p: where Ci j is the new value for the WCET of τ j , C j is the original WCET of τ j and C k is the biggest execution time of a task with priority between τ i and τ j but τ j is not included. The response time analysis applies to τ i . Note that in general the Ci j values will depend on the task under investigation. Standard response time analysis can be applied to the AR model by using the Ci j values, shown as below.

div.head: B. Non-preemptive approach
div.p: To support P-FRP, atomic execution is required. The AR model provides this, but so does the Non-Preemptive (NP) model. Below, the NP model will be introduced and compared with the AR model.

In the NP model, once a task, whatever its priority, is executing, no task can interrupt it. Figure 2 shows that if a higher priority task is released when a lower priority task is executing then the higher priority task has to wait until the lower priority task finishes. This figure shows the lower priority task executed atomically so the NP model can also be used for P-FRP. Now, we consider if the AR model can be replaced by the NP model completely. In Table III, there is a 3-tasks task-set with constrained deadlines. The response time analysis in Equation (7), given later in this paper, is used to analyse the task-set. In this task-set, the execution time of τ 1 is equal to its deadline; τ 1 therefore cannot suffer any blocking time. But he NP model will induce some blocking and hence cannot schedule this task-set.

To apply the AR model, the Ci j approach in Equation ( 1) and the response time analysis in Equation ( 2) are used. As the AR model does not have blocking time, the worst-case response time of τ 1 is 3. The worst-case response time of τ 2 is 13. Table IV is the task-set with C values for τ 3 . The worstcase response time of τ 3 is 29. The task-set can be scheduled by the AR model. The calculations are as follows:

The above example shows that the NP model does not dominate the AR model. On the other hand, the AR model does not dominate the NP model. To illustrate, Table V shows that the AR model cannot schedule the contained task-set. For the NP model, Table VI shows the task-set can be scheduled. The above examples show that the NP and AR models do not dominate each other. However, in the section on experimental evaluation, the results shows that the NP model has better schedulability than the AR model. Intuitively, a combination of them both should offer a better performance. Such a combination would be similar to an existing model called deferred preemption which combines the techniques of preemptive and non-preemptive execution. In the following section, deferred preemption will be introduced and discussed.

div.head: C. The technique of deferred preemption (DP)
div.p: Here the motivation is to improve schedulability by deferring some unnecessary preemptions. The definition of unnecessary preemption is that a higher priority task can wait until a lower priority task finishes and the higher priority task still meets its deadline. As DP is designed for non-atomicexecution systems, it cannot directly apply to P-FRP. Before adapting this technique for the AR model, DP is introduced and its analysis reviewed.

To implement DP, there are a number of approaches. In this paper, the approach from Davis and Bertogna's paper [6] is used. In their paper, a task can set the length of the final nonpreemptive region. Symbol F is used to represent the length of the final non-preemptive region. The range of
div.formula: F i for τ i is from 1 to C i . If F i = 1, τ i is fully preemptive 2 . If F i = C i , τ i is fully non-preemptive. If, for example, F i = (C i /2
div.p: ), the first half of τ i is preemptive and the last half is non-preemptive.

To illustrate, Figure 3 shows three tasks: τ 1 , τ 2 and τ 3 . The white boxes represent preemptive regions and the grey boxes represent non-preemptive regions. Task τ 1 with a fully white box is fully preemptive and F points at the end, τ 2 with a fully grey box is fully non-preemptive and F is the entire box, and Now, we introduce some equations below to analyse the DP model. In Davis and Bertogna's paper [6], the authors studied the work of Bril et al. [4], and the results are rephrased according to the notation adopted in Buttazzo et al's paper [5] to deal with the discrete time domain. The concepts of priority level-i active period, and Δ-critical instant are introduced.
The definition of priority level-i active period [6] is a continuous period of time [t 1 , t 2 ) during which tasks, of priority i or higher, are executing.

The definition of Δ-critical instant for τ i is that τ i is released simultaneously with all higher priority tasks, and a lower priority task τ k with the biggest blocking time is released a bit earlier to enter its final non-preemptive region.
Bril et al [4] showed that the worst-case response time occurs within the priority level-i active period starting at a Δcritical instant. To calculate the period, the following equation is used.
div.formula: A i = B i + ∀j∈hep(i) A i T j C j (4)
div.p: The result of A i is the length of priority level-i active period. B i is the biggest blocking time from a lower priority task. The blocking time can be calculated as follows:
div.formula: B i = max ∀l∈lp(i) (F l -1)(5)
div.p: B i is calculated by picking up the value of the final nonpreemptive region minus one.
In the priority level-i active period, there can be more than one job for a task τ i so we need to calculate the number of jobs G i . The calculation is given by:
div.formula: G i = A i T i (6
div.p: Due to more than one job per task, the response time of each job for a task must be computed. The calculation is given by:
div.formula: W NP i,g = B i +(g+1)C i -F i + ∀j∈hp (i) W i,g T j + 1 C j (7)
div.p: The result of W i,g is the start time of the final nonpreemptive region of job g (where g = 0 is the first job) for τ i . Here, we can use the technique of iteration to solve this equation. The worst-case response time of task τ i is given by:
div.formula: R i = max ∀g=0,1,2...Gi (W NP i,g + F i -gT i )(8)
div.p: The result of R i is the worst-case response time of τ i , calculated by picking the maximum value from a set of results retrieved by Equation (7).
div.formula: Task τ i is schedulable if R i ≤ D i .
div.p: To illustrate, Davis and Bertogna's paper [6] gave an example. Table VII shows a 3-tasks task-set and deadline is less than period. The priority level-3 active period for this task-set is 700 using Equation (4). First, Figure 4 shows what happens if the tasks are fully non-preemptive and the priority order is (τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 ). The top task τ 1 with the highest priority executes first but the second job is blocked by τ 3 . Task τ 3 misses its deadline for the second job. This example shows the DP model can schedule a taskset which cannot be scheduled under the NP model. Figure 3 shows as the DP model can be fully non-preemptive or fully preemptive , and therefore the DP model dominates both the preemptive and the NP models.
The following section will adapt the DP model for the technique of AR. Rather than defer preemption, we now defer abort, we therefore call it the Deferred Abort (DA) model.

div.head: III. DEFERRED ABORT
div.p: The DA model combines abort regions and non-preemptive regions in each task. The allocation of regions for a task should be be abort regions first and then non-preemptive regions. The motivation of the DA model [15] is to eliminate unnecessary aborts, reduce the abort costs and deal with the trade-off of blocking time. The definition of unnecessary aborts is that if a higher priority task does not abort a lower priority task, the system is still schedulable. To reduce the abort cost, a smaller or zero abort region can be assigned to a task. Sometimes a higher priority task cannot suffer the full blocking time from a lower priority task so there is a trade-off to decide the size of non-preemptive regions; reducing the size of non-preemptive regions means increasing the size of the abort regions.

To illustrate, Figure 6 shows that there are three types of DA tasks. The white boxes represent AR regions and the grey boxes represent non-preemptive regions. Task τ 1 with a fully white box is fully AR and F points at the end, τ 2 with a fully grey box is fully non-preemptive and F is the entire box, and τ 3 with a half white and half grey box is a DA task and F is half of the box. The benefit of using the Ci j approach (as described in Section 3) for the AR model is that the response time analysis can directly use the new execution time, regardless of the abort costs. The response time of the first job for a task is required to check if the task is schedulable or not. Intuitively, the preemptive model and the AR model using the Ci j approach are equivalent in terms of schedulability analysis, although the test for the AR model is only sufficient. By this intuition, the implementation of the DP model can be employed for the DA model by adapting the Ci j approach. Figure 7 shows there are two cases for DA tasks. The first case is that the lower priority task τ 2 executes first and the higher priority task τ 1 is released within the final non-preemptive region of τ 2 . Task τ 1 needs to wait until τ 2 completes. This case explains that when a lower priority task is about to complete, it enters the non-preemptive region to avoid abort. The second case is that a lower priority task τ 2 executes first and a higher priority task τ 1 is released soon. As τ 2 has not executed beyond point F it has not entered the non-preemptive region yet so it is aborted by τ 1 . After τ 1 is completed, τ 2 restarts.
To adapt the Ci j approach for the DA model, we adapt Equation (1):
div.formula: CDA i,j = C j + max ∀k∈hepi lpj (C k -F k )(9)
div.p: The symbol is augmented to CDA i,j . The addition of DA indicates the value is for the DA model. The C value for a task τ j when analysing τ i is the sum of the original execution time of τ j and the maximum value of execution time minus non-preemptive region of a task τ k between priority level i and j.

To introduce the equations for the DA model, the structure of the explanation for the DP model above is employed. Firstly, the priority level-i active period is obtained and then the blocking time. Afterwards, the number of jobs required to check within the active period is computed. Lastly, the equations for the response time analysis are derived.
Referring to the priority level-i active period in Equation ( 4), Ci j can be replaced by CDA i,j directly. The equation for the DA model is given by:
div.formula: A i = B i + ∀j∈hep(i) A i T j CDA i,j(10)
div.p: For the calculations of blocking time B i and the number of jobs G i , Equation ( 5) and ( 6) can still be used as the execution time C is not involved.
div.formula: B i = max ∀l∈lp(i) (F l -1) (11
G i = A i T i (12)
div.p: Now, the equation for the response time is given by:
div.formula: W i,g = B i + (g + 1)C i -F i + ∀j∈hp (i) W i,g T j + 1 CDA i,j(13)
div.p: The above equation is similar to Equation ( 7); CDA i,j is used and the result of W i,g is the start time of the final nonpreemptive region of g th job for τ i . The number of jobs is required to check that it is based on the value of the priority level-i active period. After this a set of response times for a task within the priority level-i active period is calculated, Equation ( 8) still works without any change for finding out the worst-case response time.
div.formula: R i = max ∀g=0,1,2...Gi (W NP i,g + F i -gT i )(14)
div.p: To illustrate the test, there is a 3-task task-set which will be scheduled by the models of NP, AR and DA. Deadline is less than period and the priority ordering is τ 1 highest , then τ 2 and then τ 3 . For the NP model, τ 1 cannot suffer any blocking time which is bigger than 75 as its deadline is 80 and its execution time is 5. As the execution time of τ 3 is 80, τ 1 will miss its deadline wherever τ 3 is placed. Immediately, this task-set is deemed to be unschedulable under the NP model.

For the AR model, τ 1 cannot be assigned to the lowest priority because it cannot suffer interference from τ 3 . Also τ 2 cannot assign to the lowest priority because it cannot suffer interferences from τ 1 and τ 3 . After applying the Ci j approach, τ 3 (at the lowest priority) will suffer a large interference which is obviously bigger than its deadline. The task-set is clearly not schedulable under the AR model as no task can be assigned the lowest priority.

Lastly, the DA model is applied with τ 1 and τ 2 fully nonpreemptive. For τ 3 , the AR region is 5 and the non-preemptive region is 75. The priority ordering is the same; τ 1 has the highest priority, τ 2 is at the middle and τ 3 has the lowest priority. The response time of τ 1 is 80 as it has no interference from higher priority tasks and blocking time is 75 from τ 3 . Task τ 1 is therefore schedulable at the highest priority.

For τ 2 , Table IX shows the values of CDA 2,j where τ 1 is 5 and τ 2 is 10. The response time of τ 2 is 90 as it suffers 5 time unit interference from τ 1 and 75 blocking time from τ 3 so τ 2 (just) meets its deadline.

For τ 3 , it suffers no blocking time as it is the lowest priority task. By using the values of CDA 3,j , the interferences for τ 3 are 9 from τ 1 and 14 from τ 2 so the response time is 103 (see calculation below). The DA model can schedule this task-set.
This example shows the DA model can schedule a task-set but the NP model and the AR model cannot. As tasks can be fully AR or fully non-preemptive, the DA model dominates both NP and AR models.

Now, the calculation for τ 2 is that B 2 is 75 and the active period is 90 so the number of jobs is 1. The start time of the final non-preemptive region is 80 and the worst-case response time is 90. Lastly, B 3 is 0 and the active period is 95 then the number of jobs is 1. The start time of the non-preemptive region is 80 and the worst-case response time is 103. From the calculations using Equations ( 9), ( 10) and ( 13), it mathematically shows the task-set can be scheduled by the DA model using the above approach.

div.head: A. AR or Non-preemptive Region Assignment
div.p: This subsection discusses the assignment of the final nonpreemptive region for the DA model. Previously, the equations for the response time analysis were introduced but the values of the final non-preemptive region were predefined. Now, we consider how to find out the best values of F for each task. Intuitively, tasks are initially assigned to be fully nonpreemptive as the NP model has high schedulability (mostly). However, if the system is not schedulable when the task is fully non-preemptive the non-preemptive region must be reduced and consequently an abort region is introduced.

Regardless of the priority assignment, a binary search algorithm is a simple method to deal with the problem of the final non-preemptive region assignment. To illustrate, Figures 8 and9 show how the binary search algorithm applies to a DA task.

Step 1 When a task-set is not schedulable with fully nonpreemptive, max is equal to C and min is equal to 1. Step 4.2 Again, mid is equal to (max + min)/2. The task is not schedulable with F = mid then go to Step 5.2.
Step 5.1 update the value min = mid.
Step 5.2 update the value max = mid. Step n.1 Finally, the final non-preemptive region is found when mid is pointed at max or min.
Step n.2 Finally, the final non-preemptive region is found when mid is pointed at max or min.

The motivation for using binary search for the DA model is to find the maximum length of the final non-preemptive region. Having introduced this scheme, we can return to the issue of priority assignment.

div.head: B. Priority Assignment Schemes
div.p: This subsection introduces priority assignment schemes for the DA model, which is complicated because DA tasks can be fully AR, fully non-preemptive or combined with both AR and NP. For fully AR tasks, the EUM priority assignment can be used. This is described elsewhere [18] where it is shown to be an effective priority assignment scheme for the AR model. For fully non-preemptive tasks, Audsley's algorithm [1] can be used [6] to provide an optimal priority assignment scheme. Now, we consider a new algorithm to deal with the combination of AR and NP.

For a task-set consisting of AR, NP and DA tasks, we have to consider the blocking times from low priority tasks and the interferences from high priority tasks. Mostly, nonpreemptive tasks have better schedulability than AR tasks but a NP task cannot always be used due to long blocking time and its influence on short deadline high priority tasks. For AR tasks using the Ci j approach, the priority ordering needs to be considered as the ordering of higher priority tasks is changed and that can affect the schedulability of lower priority tasks. Intuitively, the approaches to designing a new algorithm should maximise NP regions and avoid backtracking (to increase the efficiency of the scheme).

There are many possible priority assignment schemes for the DA model but a heuristic algorithm is initially given by the following. Consider a task-set Γ N = {τ 1 , τ 2 , ..., τ n } and all tasks are set to fully non-preemptive. The assignment starts with the lowest priority, P n . Each task is considered at P n , with other tasks having a higher priority. Afterwards, the binary search for the DA model is used to calculate the final non-preemptive region that is schedulable under the response time analysis using Equation (13). A set of values for P n is calculated and a schedulable task with the bigger AR region is picked. This task is given priority P n . The next assignment then occurs at P n -1 considering only those tasks that have not had their priority permanently assigned, and so on. The taskset is deemed to be unschedulable if there is no schedulable task in any of the sets. Backtracking is not needed as the tasks with a bigger AR region are assigned to lower priorities. Although it is not an optimal scheme, it is guaranteed to avoid backtracking. In this paper, we call this heuristic algorithm the MAXAR algorithm.

To illustrate, Figure 10 shows five tasks, τ 1 , τ 2 , τ 3 , τ 4 and τ 5 , regardless of the parameters of the tasks. The symbol X means the task is not schedulable at that level. The example starts in Figure 10a. The assignment starts with the lowest priority and the next column is the set of values for each task. These values are calculated based on the lowest priority level. τ 3 and τ 4 are not schedulable with the lowest priority. τ 5 with AR = 10 is picked and permanently assigned the lowest priority. The size of the final non-preemptive region is irrelevant as a biggest AR region is considered to avoid backtracking. After the lowest priority level is assigned, the example continues to Figure 10b; it shows a set of values for the second lowest priority level. This time τ 1 is chosen. In Figure 10c, τ 2 is picked; in Figure 10d: τ 4 is picked. Finally, τ 3 has the highest priority. Hence, the final priority assignment is {τ 3 , τ 4 , τ 2 , τ 1 , τ 5 }. • Deadline is equal to period.
• All tasks are periodic (includes sporadic tasks arriving at their maximum rate)
• A set of N utilisation values U i was generated by the UUniFast Algorithm [3].
• Task periods were generated between 500 and 5000 according to a log-uniform distribution 3 . And the computed value T i is assigned to τ i .
• Task execution times are:
div.formula: C i = U i • T i
div.p: • Utilisation for task-sets are ranged between 30% and 60% because some results reach 0% schedulability.
• 10000 different task-sets are generated for each utilisation rate , i.e. U = 30% generates 10000 task-sets, U = 31% generates another 10000 task-sets, and so on.

• The numbers of tasks are 5, 10 and 15. V. CONCLUSION This paper has introduced an alternative scheme, deferred abort (DA), to improve the schedulability of the AR model. The DA model combines the techniques of non-preemptive and AR. To implement the DA model, new equations are introduced, and an experiment evaluation is provided. During the discussion of the results from these experiments, it was observed that for a large number of tasks the NP model performs well. The effectiveness of the DA model is therefore best illustrated in task systems with a relatively small number of tasks. A heuristic is developed for priority assignment. It performs well; however, it is not optimal and it is possible that an improvement to the heuristic is possible. Further work will look at multiprocessor platforms in which the tasks and the system state are partitioned.

div.p: For all diagrams, the X-axis is Utilisation rate and the Yaxis is the Schedulability rate, i.e. the percentage of task-sets that were deemed schedulable. In Figure 11, the number of tasks is 5, which is small, and the schedulability is expected to be higher. The line of AR-EUM is the result of the schedulability rate for fully AR with the EUM algorithm. The line of NP-EUM is the result of fully non-preemptive with the EUM algorithm. Although EUM is not an optimal priority assignment for the NP model, it is still better than AR-EUM. The line of DA-EUM is the result of DA with the EUM algorithm. It is far better than both AR-EUM and NP-EUM. Indeed, DA dominates fully AR and fully non-preemptive. Lastly, the line of DA-MAXAR has the best performance. Although the MAXAR algorithm is a heuristic, the result shows a big improvement at 60% utilisation. In Figure 12, the number of tasks is 10. The line of AR-EUM has dropped as expected, and it reaches 0% schedulability at 50% utilisation. The line of NP-EUM is degraded too but it has not reached 0% schedulability before 60% utilisation. The line of DA-EUM has less schedulability than before. Now the line of DA-MAXAR has better schedulability than the result from 5-tasks task-sets. The result is not expected, so further analysis and discussion will follow.

In Figure 13, the number of tasks is 15 which is bigger. The line of AR-EUM has very poor performance which also reaches 0% schedulability at 40% utilisation. The line of NP-EUM finally reaches 0% schedulability at 60% utilisation. The The results of DA-MAXAR from above are not expected. When the number of tasks is increased, the schedulability also increases. In the meantime, the execution times of tasks will be smaller relatively. The NP model gets the benefit of small execution times because the blocking times will be smaller. To illustrate, Figure 14 shows three cases of different numbers of tasks. The utilisation of the system is set to 60%. When the number of tasks is 3, each task has five boxes for its execution time. When the number of tasks is 5, the execution time of each task is three boxes. When the number of tasks is 15, only one box represent the execution time for each task. By this example, the blocking time is very small in the task-set with N = 15. To show this is correct, a further experiment is done and it is given below.
The experiment below shows that the NP model has an advantage with a bigger number of tasks. For the fully nonpreemptive we now use the optimal Audsley's algorithm [1] (denoted as NP-AA).
In Figure 15 for 5 tasks, the line of NP-AA is better than the line of DA-EUM because of the optimal priority assignment for fully non-preemptive. The line of DA-MAXAR is still the best.
In Figure 16, the number of tasks is 10. Both lines of NP-AA and DA-MAXAR are increased.
